- Model consistently overestimates prices in early forecast windows, especially after sharp spikes or volatility; reduce initial forecast peaks by 5–10%.
- After a significant price spike, model tends to overshoot and fail to correct downward; apply a “cool-down” adjustment: subtract 1–2% per subsequent day if sentiment remains neutral or negative.
- When sentiment history is uniformly zero (no market sentiment signal), model should not assume momentum; instead, anchor forecast to recent 7–14 day moving average.
- Model exhibits strong mean reversion bias in mid-to-late forecast horizon (days 15–30), but undercorrects; apply a “reversion buffer” — if forecast is >1.5σ above recent mean, reduce by 0.5–1.0σ.
- If true outcome shows sudden drop after a forecast peak, model often fails to recognize it as a “reversal event”; add a “reversal trigger” rule: if true price drops >3% from peak within 3 days, reduce forecast by 2–4% for next 5 days.
- Sentiment history is always zero — no behavioral signal — so model should not assume sentiment-driven drift; treat as “neutral market” and avoid overfitting to past momentum.
